claims.sentence: The NHS knee pain page lists sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, damage to the meniscus or cartilage, a dislocated kneecap, osteoarthritis, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter disease.
claims.evidence: Search text for the NHS page lists sprains/strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout (with septic arthritis in same row), Osgood-Schlatter's. Osteoarthritis and 'cartilage' not seen in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease.

claims.sentence: Overuse or injury often causes sudden knee pain.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text links sprains/strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting, often during exercise; no 'often causes sudden knee pain' statement seen.
claims.newSentence: The NHS knee pain page links sprains and strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting the knee, often during exercise.

claims.sentence: An NHS trust leaflet describes osteoarthritis as cartilage gradually worn away with age or after injury, mainly at the points of greatest pressure.
claims.evidence: Newcastle OA leaflet search text did not mention cartilage wearing away.

claims.sentence: It can cause pain, stiffness, loss of movement, swelling and deformity.
claims.evidence: Newcastle leaflet text retrieved lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling; loss of movement and deformity not seen.
claims.newSentence: An NHS trust leaflet lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling as symptoms of osteoarthritis.

claims.sentence: NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: exact cause unknown, likely a combination; risk factors include age-related changes, previous injury, repetitive or physical work, genetics, being overweight.

claims.sentence: Imaging and symptoms do not always match, because many people with signs of osteoarthritis on an X-ray have very mild symptoms or none.
claims.evidence: NHS inform not shown saying this. An RJAH NHS trust page says over half of people over 65 show changes on X-ray but this does not necessarily correlate with symptoms; 'very mild or none' overstated; attribution wrong.
claims.newSentence: An NHS trust page says changes seen on an X-ray do not necessarily match how bad the symptoms are.

claims.sentence: NHS sources say that strengthening the thigh muscles is commonly recommended for knee osteoarthritis, and that exercise does not speed up the arthritis.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: strengthening muscles around the knee helps manage symptoms. Thigh strengthening comes from Leeds and Royal Berkshire trust leaflets. 'Exercise does not speed up the arthritis' not found.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says strengthening the muscles around the knee helps manage osteoarthritis symptoms.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes reducing weight on the knee, using a cold pack wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, and taking paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain.
claims.evidence: Main NHS advice: reduce weight on knee, ice pack, painkillers. The tea-towel, 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours detail came from the NHS 111 Wales page, not nhs.uk, and other trusts give different timings; paracetamol/ibuprofen listed as standard options.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.

claims.sentence: Staying gently active is also advised.
claims.evidence: Not found on the NHS page; only trust pages mention gentle exercise, with differing wording.

claims.sentence: An NHS trust says keeping active and gradually returning to usual activities helps recovery.
claims.evidence: UHCW page appeared in results but no text supporting this was retrieved.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises a GP visit if knee pain does not improve within a few weeks.
claims.evidence: Not confirmed as nhs.uk text; retrieved wording came from Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance (GP visit suggested if not eased within a few weeks). Attribution changed.
claims.newSentence: Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks.

claims.sentence: The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP.
claims.evidence: NHS page: most adults in England can refer themselves to community MSK services; availability varies, GP registration needed. Better URL for the claim.

claims.sentence: An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee.
claims.evidence: Sherwood Forest trust leaflet: physiotherapy is the mainstay of treatment for conditions related to the front of the knee.

claims.sentence: Management of knee osteoarthritis includes exercise programmes, pain relief and footwear advice, according to an NHS trust.
claims.evidence: Newcastle leaflet text retrieved covers regular exercise, paracetamol/NSAIDs and losing a small amount of body fat; footwear not seen there.
claims.newSentence: An NHS trust leaflet on hip and knee osteoarthritis describes regular exercise, over-the-counter pain relief and losing a small amount of body fat.

claims.sentence: A guide from another trust mentions an MRI scan if a ligament or meniscus tear could be the cause.
claims.evidence: Leeds page appeared in results but MRI statement not retrieved.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.
claims.evidence: Search text: NHS 111 advice applies if the knee is badly swollen or misshapen, or hot and red with a high temperature; redness/heat around joint can signal infection. Retrieved wording says 'high' not 'very high' temperature; check.

claims.sentence: An NHS trust A&E leaflet advises attending A&E after a high-impact injury with immediate swelling, a pop, severe pain or inability to put weight on the leg, or for a knee or leg that looks deformed.
claims.evidence: Sussex A&E leaflet search text did not contain this; it says to seek GP or 111 review if pain, warmth or swelling worsen. Unable to confirm A&E route.

claims.sentence: Most knee pain settles with gentle activity, and a GP visit is advised if it does not improve, while a badly swollen or hot, red knee needs NHS 111.
claims.evidence: 'Most settles with gentle activity' not sourced (trust leaflet: usually resolves in 6-12 weeks without treatment). 'Hot, red knee needs 111' omits the high temperature condition.
claims.newSentence: Knee pain can often be treated at home; a GP visit is suggested if it has not eased within a few weeks, and the NHS advises calling 111 for a badly swollen knee or one that is hot and red with a high temperature.

notes: All 8 searches used. Search returned blended summaries, so nhs.uk page text itself was not seen verbatim; 'supported' rests on those summaries. Main gap: the draft's emergency route (A&E) is unsupported; retrieved NHS text says 111 for cannot bear weight, badly swollen, misshapen or hot/red with high temperature, so consider adding that 111 line (cannot put weight on leg) in a corrected body[3]. Osteoarthritis was not confirmed in the NHS page cause list. Self-care timings (20 min every 2 to 3 hours) came from NHS 111 Wales, not nhs.uk. Did not check site's own symptom pages.
